props.title: Crowhaven Farm
props.initialSlug: Woman inherits cursed farm with deadly witch legacy

sections.content: Crowhaven Farm (1970) stands as a haunting entry in the golden age of made-for-TV horror films, alongside classics like Dark Night of the Scarecrow (1981) and Don't Be Afraid of the Dark (1973). This ABC Movie of the Week tapped into America's renewed fascination with witchcraft and colonial persecution, arriving in the wake of Rosemary's Baby (1968). The film's plot about a modern couple inheriting a cursed Massachusetts farm cleverly interweaves reincarnation with Salem Witch Trial themes, predating similar supernatural inheritance stories like The Amityville Horror (1979).

sections.content: Director Walter Grauman brought television horror expertise from directing episodes of The Twilight Zone (1959-1964), crafting effective scares despite broadcast limitations. Hope Lange's lead performance as Maggie Porter channels the same vulnerable-yet-determined energy that made The Ghost and Mrs. Muir (1968-1970) compelling. The film's past-life regression scenes were groundbreaking for TV horror, influencing later works like Audrey Rose (1977).

Crowhaven Farm draws power from its authentic New England locations and period-accurate witch trial references, setting a template for regional horror that would later influence films like The Witch (2015). The movie's themes of generational guilt and karmic retribution echo through later witch-themed horror like Lords of Salem (2012) and The Covenant (2006). SUBHEAD: Television Horror's Golden Age

sections.content: The success of Crowhaven Farm helped establish ABC's Movie of the Week format as a proving ground for horror, leading to gems like Trilogy of Terror (1975) and Bad Ronald (1974). These productions often matched theatrical releases in quality while working within television's content restrictions, forcing creative approaches to supernatural horror that emphasized psychological dread over graphic violence.
